Date: 2026-09-04

Location: Zoom

Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Das (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (NebulaPay Eng Mgmt), Sara Gomez (NebulaPay ML Infra), Tom Liu (NebulaPay SRE), Ellen Park (NebulaPay Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):

- Next: share spreadsheet with sweep results, schedule runtime deep-dive.

Topics: TTFT (time-to-first-token) trends, streaming handshake lag, seqlen corridor thresholds, kernel choice hedging, prefix/KV cache impact, SLA implications, cost tradeoffs.

Transcript body (note: auto-transcript, some mis-words likely):
[00:00] Maya Chen: alright everyone thanks for joining on time, um this is the weekly sync for the NebulaPay pilot, main goals today are — quick review of last week's runs and then handoff for the seqlen corridor sweep.
[00:18] Ravi Patel: thanks Maya, yeah we ran the two-hour load window you asked for, got some interesting first-byte spikes around 95th pct when payloads had long seqlen tails.
[00:30] Liam O'Connor: yeah that's consistent with what we saw in the staging harness, the microbursts push some requests off the fastpath kernel and then you get a cascade on fallback, which bumps TTFT.
[00:45] Sara Gomez: quick question — when you say fastpath kernel, are we talking about the optimized fused-attn path or the quantized CUDA kernel? I wasn't sure which mapping Redwood used in that test.
[01:00] Priya Das: good point, the run we flagged used the fused attention path for seqlen <=8, then a different fallback kernel for >8. We call it the 'hedge' config.
[01:12] Tom Liu: there was one run where the transcript log spelled hedging as 'edging' which confused our automation, minor but FYI.
[01:20] Maya Chen: heh yeah auto-transcripts do that. Ok, quick numbers — from the spreadsheet, avg TTFT improved ~22% on the hybrid hedging config, but the 99th still had ~180ms spikes under microbursts.
[01:36] Ellen Park: is that 180ms measured at the SDK or at our edge? we need cross-checks because our client sees ~240ms.
[01:44] Liam O'Connor: recorded at the Redwood ingress, so end-to-end will add your network egress. We should align traces — Sara can upload the SDK-side capture and we'll correlate.
[01:55] Sara Gomez: yes we'll upload. we'll also include the seqlen histograms per endpoint.
[02:06] Ravi Patel: our main success criteria for pilot phase 2 is: <120ms p95 TTFT for our chat flows and bounded p99 under 200ms. Is that still achievable?
[02:18] Maya Chen: yes that's our target too. With corridor thresholds tuned and prefix caching enabled most of the time, it's feasible. We just need to verify under your actual token distribution.
[02:30] Tom Liu: question — does prefix cache help for streaming scenarios or only for cached completions?
[02:38] Priya Das: prefix cache helps whenever there's repeated prompt prefixes, for streaming you still benefit because the KV cache short-circuits computation on earlier layers. But it depends on alignment of requests.
[02:50] Ravi Patel: we don't have much repeated prefix today, more dynamic user prompts, so we'll probably rely on seqlen corridor and kernel hedging.
[03:00] Liam O'Connor: that's fine; corridor is a low-friction config: we route requests with predicted out-seqlen <=8 to the fastpath and route rest to fallback, this avoids the expensive kernel-switch during generation.
[03:16] Sara Gomez: how do you predict out-seqlen? we don't want heavy precompute.
[03:24] Priya Das: two lightweight heuristics: 1) input tokens + mean completions from trace, 2) inline length-limit classifier that costs ~0.2ms. We use the simpler heuristic for now.
[03:37] Ravi Patel: hmm classifier seems like extra infra — can we start with static thresholds and then move to classifier if needed?
[03:44] Maya Chen: absolutely, start simple. That's why seqlen corridor sweep is helpful — pick candidate thresholds (2,4,8,16) and measure hit-rate, cost, and TTFT.
[03:58] Tom Liu: about streaming handshake — we've been seeing small jitter at the first chunk (~30-60ms) even when TTFT is low. Could that be gRPC windowing?
[04:08] Liam O'Connor: possible, also our streaming buffer size and client chunking interact. We'll log the handshake timing separately.
[04:16] Ellen Park: competitor note — one vendor we evaluated had a single-pipeline approach which avoided kernel switching but paid in steady-state cost; curious if Redwood's hedging is cost-effective.
[04:28] Maya Chen: the tradeoff is exactly that: hedge gives latency without large cost increase because most traffic stays on fastpath. We'll add cost column to the sweep.
[04:36] Ravi Patel: okay let's talk about the microbenchmark Liam ran — what kernels did you compare?
[04:42] Liam O'Connor: compared fused-attn fastpath, quantized matmul kernel, and an experimental tiled kernel. The tiled kernel had lower variability on longer sequences but slightly higher median.
[04:54] Priya Das: note: the experimental tiled kernel isn't in the hosted default yet; it's in the dedicated branch. We can run it for you under the pilot dedicated pool if you want.
[05:06] Sara Gomez: NebulaPay is tentatively interested in dedicated if we can certify the throughput. Can you quote the commit needed for a small reserved capacity?
[05:14] Maya Chen: yes we can put a small burst plan on the table, I'll follow up with pricing.
[05:19] Ravi Patel: for this week, the important piece is the seqlen sweep and matching traces. Any blockers?
[05:26] Sara Gomez: just permissions to upload traces — security needs the exact S3 path.
[05:30] Maya Chen: I'll send the exact signed URL and the minimal retention policy we need.
[05:36] Tom Liu: FYI security asked about KMS for logs, do you support customer-managed keys?
[05:42] Liam O'Connor: yes for Private we do; for Hosted we offer KMS integration and can support CMKs for audit logs. We'll share the security pack after.
[05:52] Ravi Patel: also can you remind us of the default queueing model — is it continuous batching or fixed-time windows?
[06:00] Priya Das: continuous batching in the runtime, with an empirical max batch ms; but for latency SLOs we tune the thresholds so the batch wait is minimal.
[06:10] Ellen Park: one operational ask — if a fallback kernel blows up, do you have automatic rollback? we don't want production surprises.
[06:18] Liam O'Connor: yes we have route hedging and automatic fallback to a safe model variant; also alerting and circuit-breaker. We'll add a canary for the tiled kernel.
[06:28] Maya Chen: okay quick demo of the spreadsheet (screen share noted in meeting).
[06:34] [screen share noises]
[06:40] Liam O'Connor: here is the sweep table: columns are seqlen_threshold, hit_rate_fastpath, p50_ttft, p95_ttft, p99_ttft, cost_multiplier. For seqlen <=8 the hit rate 78% on our synthetic, p95 drops to 90ms, p99 ~160ms, cost +6%.
[06:58] Ravi Patel: that 6% cost is acceptable. how does that change if we enable prefix cache at 10% hit?
[07:06] Priya Das: you'd see effective cost drop because cached prefixes short-circuit compute, for the same traffic pattern cost could be net -2% while p95 improves further.
[07:16] Sara Gomez: we don't have that many repeats, but some channels (notifications templates) would benefit.
[07:22] Tom Liu: where do we see the experiments' raw logs?
[07:26] Liam O'Connor: in the shared spreadsheet there's links to the S3 logs and the kbench outputs.
[07:32] Ellen Park: request — can Redwood include a column that estimates end-to-end with our avg egress?
[07:38] Maya Chen: yes we'll add an 'estimated client RTT' column.
[07:42] Ravi Patel: good. I want to call out edge-case: we have a subset of calls with long system prompts (200+ tokens) with short completions; those flip the prediction and often go to fallback. any suggestion?
[07:55] Liam O'Connor: in that case we can base corridor on predicted generation length (not total seqlen) or implement an override: if input prompt > N tokens, route to tiled kernel because the batch cost is different.
[08:06] Priya Das: we should capture those in the trace export as a separate filter so we can present recommendations.
[08:12] Sara Gomez: will do.
[08:16] Maya Chen: ok wrapping toward next steps — restate: NebulaPay to upload traces (Sara), Redwood to run full seqlen corridor sweep and kernel microbenchmarks (Liam), Maya to share pricing and signed upload URL (Maya).
[08:30] Ravi Patel: timeline?
[08:32] Maya Chen: aims: traces by 2026-09-08, bench results and spreadsheet by 2026-09-10, schedule kernel deep dive for week of 2026-09-13.
[08:40] Tom Liu: sounds good. any risks to call out?
[08:44] Liam O'Connor: risk: if your real traffic has higher variance than test harness, p99 might still exceed 200ms — mitigation is to run a short production canary.
[08:55] Ellen Park: we'll probably ask for a 48-hour canary on small dedicated capacity if numbers align.
[09:02] Maya Chen: perfect, we'll prepare the canary run plan if the sweep looks good.
[09:08] Ravi Patel: thanks team.
[09:10] Meeting end / quick recap ran through next steps and owners.
